sections.section_title: Clinical Background and Pathophysiology Relevant to the Case
sections.description: Builds core knowledge to interpret this presentation by summarizing Behçet’s disease (BD), neurological Behçet’s disease (neuro-BD), and the physiology of SIADH, with a focus on mechanisms directly pertinent to this case.
subtopics: Behçet’s disease overview: mucocutaneous triad (oral/genital ulcers, skin lesions), multisystem vasculitis nature, typical disease course
HLA-B51: epidemiologic association vs. non-diagnostic role in individual patients
Neuro-Behçet’s disease: parenchymal vs non-parenchymal phenotypes; acute meningoencephalitis presentations; typical brainstem involvement; frequency and timing relative to BD onset
CSF and imaging in acute neuro-BD: aseptic meningitis patterns; normal early MRI does not exclude neuro-BD
SIADH physiology: ADH regulation, diagnostic criteria, and common CNS inflammatory triggers
Cytokine–neuroendocrine link: IL-6 and other inflammatory mediators promoting ADH release; relevance to neuroinflammation and BD
Clinical consequences of hyponatraemia pertinent to this case: hiccups as a clue, risk of rhabdomyolysis, and neurologic symptom amplification

sections.description: Traces the initial clinical picture and early differential, highlighting how the team prioritized urgent possibilities and structured the workup before the BD and neuro-BD diagnoses crystallized.
subtopics: Initial symptoms and exam: fever, headache, malaise, hiccups, arthralgia; oral aphthae and folliculitis-like rash; tachycardia; euvolemic status

Early differential diagnosis: infectious meningoencephalitis (HSV/VZV, bacterial, TB), systemic inflammatory diseases, malignancy (CNS lymphoma), endocrine/metabolic causes of hyponatraemia, drug-induced etiologies
Baseline labs: markedly elevated CRP/ESR; hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality; high urine osmolality and urine Na; normal renal, thyroid, and adrenal function
Imaging and CSF: normal brain MRI early; CSF with mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, negative infectious studies—consistent with aseptic meningitis
Interim management aligned with provisional diagnoses: empiric cefepime and acyclovir pending exclusion of bacterial/viral CNS infection
Evolution of mucocutaneous findings: emergence of painful genital ulcer refining suspicion for systemic BD

sections.section_title: Nailing the Diagnoses: Applying Criteria and Diagnostic Reasoning
sections.description: Details how the final diagnoses of definite BD, acute neuro-BD, and SIADH were established, emphasizing exclusion of mimics, structured criteria, and synthesis of disparate data.
subtopics: Definite BD classification: International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease scoring (oral aphthae 2, genital aphthosis 2, folliculitis-like rash 1; total 5 ≥ 4)
Acute neuro-BD: CNS symptoms with concurrent BD; recognition that normal MRI early does not rule out neuro-BD; CSF aseptic meningitis pattern

SIADH confirmation: hypotonic hyponatraemia, inappropriately concentrated urine, elevated urine sodium, clinical euvolaemia, normal thyroid/adrenal/renal function, elevated ADH; absence of diuretics or offending drugs

Excluding mimics: negative CSF PCR/cultures for HSV/VZV/bacteria/TB; non-contributory imaging for mass lesions; negative cytology; non-specific sIL-2R and normal ACE/lysozyme reducing likelihood of lymphoma or neurosarcoidosis
Pathophysiologic synthesis: plausible IL-6–mediated CNS inflammation driving ADH release in acute neuro-BD; aligning timing of SIADH with neuroinflammatory phase

sections.description: Explains therapeutic decisions, including antimicrobial stewardship, BD/neuro-BD anti-inflammatory choices, and safe correction of SIADH-related hyponatraemia, with attention to complications and comorbidities.
subtopics: Empiric therapy and de-escalation: starting cefepime/acyclovir while infection was unexcluded; timely discontinuation after negative studies

Choice of colchicine monotherapy: mechanism (neutrophil migration inhibition; IL-1β/IL-6 downregulation); typical use for mucocutaneous BD; rationale for trial in mild acute neuro-BD when steroid-sparing desired
Context of standard care: usual role of high-dose corticosteroids and immunosuppressants in acute neuro-BD; evidence base vs this case’s atypical favorable response

SIADH management: fluid restriction (<800 mL/day), frequent sodium monitoring, principles to avoid rapid correction (limits for daily rise), indications for hypertonic saline or vaptans if severe/symptomatic or refractory
Monitoring for complications: checking CK and managing rhabdomyolysis risk; recognizing hiccups as a marker of severe hyponatraemia
Supportive and comorbidity care: topical steroids for oral aphthae; silver sulfadiazine for ulcers; rehabilitation for deconditioning; staged diabetes optimization after acute phase

sections.section_title: Outcomes, Follow-up, and Key Clinical Lessons
sections.description: Summarizes the patient’s clinical course and crystallizes practice-oriented takeaways for recognizing and managing concurrent neuro-BD and SIADH.
subtopics: Clinical trajectory: rapid symptomatic improvement after colchicine; normalization of sodium and ADH; resolution of CK elevation; discharge after 1 month
Long-term outcome: 4-year remission on colchicine without neuro recurrences; later initiation of biguanide therapy with good glycaemic control

Follow-up priorities: monitoring for BD relapse (mucocutaneous, ocular, neurologic), periodic neurologic assessment, sodium checks if CNS symptoms recur, ophthalmology screening despite initial absence of uveitis

Teaching points and pitfalls: consider neuro-BD in BD patients with nonspecific CNS symptoms; normal early MRI does not exclude neuro-BD; integrate BD criteria promptly as mucocutaneous signs evolve; recognize SIADH via lab triad and clinical euvolaemia; hiccups/rhabdomyolysis as hyponatraemia clues; avoid indiscriminate testing—anchor on clinical context
When to escalate: indications to add corticosteroids or immunosuppressants in neuro-BD (focal deficits, radiographic lesions, severe or progressive course, treatment failure)
